Clinical Reference

Hepatorenal Syndrome

On this page
Hepatorenal syndrome is kidney failure caused by a circulation problem, not a kidney problem — in advanced cirrhosis the splanchnic arteries dilate so widely that the effective arterial blood volume collapses, the kidney is clamped shut by RAAS, sympathetic outflow and ADH, and the creatinine climbs even though the kidney tissue itself is nearly normal.
Functional & potentially reversible Diagnosis of exclusion Untreated: survival measured in days to weeks Terlipressin + albumin · transplant is the cure
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story, step by step

Everything in this guide follows from one idea: in hepatorenal syndrome the kidney is a bystander. If you took that kidney out and transplanted it into someone with a healthy liver, it would work. If you gave the patient a new liver, the same kidney would recover. The lesion is in the circulation, and the kidney is simply the organ that pays the price first.

Step 1 — Fibrosis raises portal pressure

Cirrhotic nodules and fibrous septa mechanically obstruct sinusoidal flow, and activated stellate cells contract around the sinusoids. Portal pressure rises. Once the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) exceeds 10 mm Hg the patient has clinically significant portal hypertension and can start forming varices and ascites; above ~12 mm Hg ascites becomes common.

Step 2 — Portal hypertension dilates the splanchnic arteries

High flow and shear stress on the splanchnic endothelium upregulate endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Nitric oxide — joined by carbon monoxide and endocannabinoids — relaxes splanchnic arteriolar smooth muscle. The mesenteric arterial bed becomes an enormous low-resistance reservoir. This is the pivotal event: systemic vascular resistance falls, and blood pools in the gut circulation.

Step 3 — Effective arterial blood volume collapses

Total body water is increased (that is the ascites and the edema), yet the volume the arterial baroreceptors actually sense is low. This paradox — an overfilled patient with an underfilled arterial tree — is the single most important concept in the disease, and it explains why giving furosemide feels reasonable and is often exactly wrong.

Step 4 — The body compensates, and the compensation is what harms the kidney

Unloaded carotid and renal baroreceptors trigger three vasoconstrictor systems at once:

  • Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone. Angiotensin II constricts the renal efferent > afferent arteriole; aldosterone drives avid distal sodium reabsorption → ascites and edema, and a urine sodium that falls below 10 mEq/L.
  • Sympathetic nervous system. Direct renal nerve traffic constricts the afferent arteriole and further stimulates renin.
  • Non-osmotic ADH (vasopressin) release. Free-water retention out of proportion to sodium → the dilutional hyponatremia that marks advanced disease and independently predicts death.

Early on, locally produced renal vasodilator prostaglandins hold the afferent arteriole open and preserve GFR. This is precisely why an NSAID can convert a compensated patient into anuric HRS within a day — it removes the last defense.

Step 5 — Autoregulation fails, and creatinine finally moves

GFR is defended until the vasoconstrictor load overwhelms renal autoregulation; then function falls off a cliff. That is why HRS looks like it appears "suddenly" after months of stable labs, and why the creatinine trend over days matters more than any single value.

The modern additions — it is not purely hemodynamic

  • Systemic inflammation. A leaky, congested gut translocates bacteria and bacterial products. LPS engaging TLR4 drives cytokine release that both worsens vasodilation and injures tubules directly. This is why infection is the most common trigger, and why SBP is the classic precipitant.
  • Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy. Cardiac output is high but cannot rise further when demanded; a blunted contractile reserve means the heart cannot rescue the falling effective volume.
  • Relative adrenal insufficiency is common in advanced cirrhosis and contributes to vasopressor-resistant hypotension.
  • Tubular injury overlaps. The old dogma of a histologically pristine kidney is only approximately true — many patients have some degree of concurrent tubular injury, which is why urinary biomarkers and the response to treatment are imperfect discriminators.
Imagine the circulation as a closed loop of garden hose. Cirrhosis slashes a huge opening in the section running through the gut, so that stretch of hose balloons out. The heart responds by pumping harder — cardiac output goes up — but the pressure at the far end of the loop, where the kidney sits, keeps falling, because all the volume is sitting in the ballooned segment. The body's only reflex is to clamp down every other hose in the system, and the kidney's hose is the one it clamps hardest. Vasoconstrictors shrink the ballooned segment back down. Albumin puts more water into the loop. Only a new liver stops the slashing.
The core lesion is distribution, not pump failure: cardiac output is high, yet the arterial tree that matters is underfilled. Vasoconstrictors work by re-narrowing the splanchnic pipe in panel B.
The complete cascade. Green boxes are the three places we can intervene — and each one maps to a specific arrow, not to "the kidney."
Why HRS appears late and suddenly: GFR is defended by autoregulation until the vasoconstrictor load overwhelms it — then creatinine climbs over days, not months.
Cut surface of a cirrhotic liver: diffuse micronodularity with fatty change. This architecture is what obstructs sinusoidal flow and raises portal pressure — step 1 of the cascade.
CDC / Dr. Edwin P. Ewing, Jr., CC0 — Wikimedia Commons, Gross pathology of alcoholic liver cirrhosis.jpg
Masson trichrome: regenerative nodules encircled by blue collagen septa. The septa are the mechanical resistance; the stellate cells within them add a contractile, dynamic component.
Ed Uthman (Houston, TX), CC BY 2.0 — Wikimedia Commons, Cirrhosis of the liver (trichrome stain).jpg
The point of the whole disease. This is essentially what the kidney looks like in HRS — a normal glomerulus and preserved tubules. There is no glomerulonephritis, no vasculitis, no necrosis to find. The organ is structurally intact and functionally strangled, which is exactly why reversing the circulation reverses the "renal failure."
Nephron, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons, Benign kidney -- intermed mag.jpg
Contrast with acute tubular necrosis — flattened, vacuolated tubular epithelium with luminal debris. ATN is the main structural mimic of HRS and accounts for roughly 14–35% of AKI in cirrhosis (AASLD 2021); distinguishing the two at the bedside is the central diagnostic problem.
Amadalvarez, CC BY-SA 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons, Necrosi tubular aguda renal.IMG 1779.JPG
Every therapy in this guide maps to one arrow in the cascade above. Terlipressin is a V1a receptor agonist — V1a receptors are densely expressed on splanchnic vascular smooth muscle and sparsely on renal vessels, so it constricts the ballooned segment while largely sparing the kidney. Norepinephrine does the same job through α1 receptors, less selectively. Midodrine (α1 agonist) plus octreotide (inhibits splanchnic vasodilator peptides such as glucagon) attack the same step orally/subcutaneously, but far more weakly. Albumin is not merely oncotic — it also binds nitric oxide, bilirubin, bile acids and endotoxin, and stabilizes the endothelium, which is why 25% albumin outperforms an equivalent volume of crystalloid. TIPS lowers portal pressure itself, removing the upstream stimulus. NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and aminoglycosides each remove a defense or add an insult at the renal arteriole — which is why the first order in suspected HRS is a stop order. Iodinated contrast belongs on that stop list for a different reason: modern prospective data put its nephrotoxic risk in cirrhosis close to baseline, but recent contrast exposure is an explicit exclusion in the diagnostic criteria, so a contrast study can cost you the diagnosis even when it does not harm the kidney.

Definitions & criteria

📖

Naming: type 1 / type 2 are dead

The old split into "type 1" (rapid) and "type 2" (slow, with refractory ascites) has been replaced by a time-based nomenclature aligned with how we classify kidney injury everywhere else. The historical type-1 definition — a doubling of creatinine to >2.5 mg/dL within 2 weeks — was abandoned because it forced clinicians to wait for a very high creatinine before treating, by which time response rates collapse.

Current termOld termDefinitionTypical picture
HRS-AKIHRS type 1Meets AKI criteria (below)Rapid rise over days, usually a precipitant (infection, bleed, large-volume tap without albumin); the emergency
HRS-AKDHRS type 2 (part)Kidney dysfunction <90 days not meeting AKI criteria — eGFR <60 or a lesser creatinine riseSmoldering; usually with refractory ascites
HRS-CKDHRS type 2 (part)Persisting >90 daysChronic; drives the simultaneous liver–kidney transplant conversation

Nomenclature per the ADQI/ICA 2024 joint consensus (Nadim et al., J Hepatol 2024): "HRS for less than 90 days would be classified as HRS-AKD, while HRS persisting for more than 90 days would be classified as HRS-CKD."

📏

Staging AKI in cirrhosis (ICA / KDIGO)

AKI is diagnosed by a rise in serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, or ≥50% from baseline known or presumed to have occurred within the prior 7 days. The 2024 ADQI/ICA consensus adds a urine-output limb: ≤0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 hours.

Baseline = a stable creatinine within the previous 3 months. If no prior value exists, AASLD is explicit: a formal diagnosis of AKI can only be made if the creatinine continues to rise during the hospitalization.

StageCreatinine criterionWhat it means for you
1Rise ≥0.3 mg/dL up to 2× baselineStop the offenders, look for the trigger, volume-challenge
1AStage 1 with creatinine <1.5 mg/dLOften resolves with removal of the insult alone
1BStage 1 with creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dLMaterially worse outcomes — treat like stage 2
22× to 3× baselineVasoconstrictor territory if HRS-AKI
3>3× baseline, or creatinine >4.0 mg/dL with an acute rise ≥0.3 mg/dL, or starting RRTICU-level illness; response rates fall steeply

Staging per AASLD 2021 Table 10. On 1A/1B, AASLD notes the writing group was split — some favored the split because stage-1 patients with creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL "fared significantly worse," others held that the effect of creatinine is continuous. Either way, the absolute creatinine within stage 1 carries real prognostic weight.

✅

Diagnosing HRS-AKI — and what changed in 2024

HRS-AKI has always been a diagnosis of exclusion. You are never proving HRS; you are running out of alternatives. Two criteria sets are currently in play, and it is worth knowing both — most US order sets still encode the AASLD 2021 version, while the 2024 consensus is where the field is moving.

CriterionAASLD 2021 (Table 11)ADQI / ICA 2024 consensus
SubstrateCirrhosis with ascitesCirrhosis with ascites (unchanged)
Kidney injuryAKI by ICA-AKI criteria (creatinine only)Creatinine criteria and/or urine output ≤0.5 mL/kg × ≥6 h
Volume trialNo response after 2 consecutive days of diuretic withdrawal plus albumin 1 g/kg/dayNo improvement within 24 h after adequate volume resuscitation "when clinically indicated" — the mandatory 48-hour albumin trial is explicitly dropped
ShockAbsence of shockFolded into "no strong evidence for an alternative explanation"
NephrotoxinsNo current/recent NSAIDs, aminoglycosides or iodinated contrastFolded into the same clause
Structural injuryNo proteinuria >500 mg/day, no microhematuria >50 RBC/hpf, normal renal ultrasoundNot retained as hard cutoffs in the criteria themselves — used as clinical evidence of an alternative cause
The 2024 change is the clinically important one. The consensus states plainly: "We recommend against systematic administration of albumin for 48 h as a requisite for the diagnosis of HRS-AKI (strong recommendation, grade D)." The rationale is that two days of watching a rising creatinine before starting a vasoconstrictor costs response rates and lives — and terlipressin works far better at lower creatinine. If the patient is clearly not volume-responsive and clearly has no alternative cause, you do not have to run the clock out.
Three things masquerade as HRS and will not respond to terlipressin: ATN (granular/muddy-brown casts, often after shock or a nephrotoxin), bile cast nephropathy (profound hyperbilirubinemia — typically bilirubin well above 20 mg/dL — with bile-stained casts), and abdominal compartment syndrome from tense ascites (relieved by paracentesis, not vasoconstrictors). Check a bladder pressure if the abdomen is drum-tight and the urine output fell abruptly.

Presentation & differential

🔍

Symptoms and signs — frequency and mechanism

Frequency key: >70% · 40–70% · 15–40% · <15%

Feature~FrequencyWhy it happens
Ascites100%
required for diagnosis		Portal hypertension + splanchnic vasodilation + avid renal Na⁺/H₂O retention + hypoalbuminemia. AASLD Table 11 opens with "cirrhosis with ascites" — no ascites, no HRS.
Fatigue, nausea, anorexiaVery commonUremia, hyponatremia, systemic inflammation, sarcopenia. Non-specific and easily dismissed.
Oliguria~50–80%Collapse of renal blood flow and GFR plus maximal ADH- and aldosterone-driven reabsorption. AASLD: "oliguria is associated with poor prognosis."
Jaundice~50–80%Hepatocellular failure and cholestasis. Mechanistically important, not just cosmetic — severe cholestasis worsens renal function through bile-salt tubular toxicity.
Hyponatremia (Na ≤135)49%
in cirrhosis + ascites		Non-osmotic ADH release → free-water retention out of proportion to sodium. 22% have Na ≤130, which carries OR 3.5 for developing HRS.
Peripheral edema~50%Same sodium and water retention, plus low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia.
Weight gain / abdominal distensionCommonFluid accumulation. Anchor number: the peritoneum reabsorbs only ~500 mL/day, which is why diuresis targets are capped.
Hypotension / low MAPCommonLow systemic vascular resistance from splanchnic vasodilation, with a cardiac output that cannot rise further. MAP is the key modifiable target.
Muscle crampsCommonAASLD notes they are common (especially on diuretics) and meaningfully hurt quality of life, but the mechanism "remains unclear" — likely volume/electrolyte shifts plus impaired muscle energy metabolism.
SplenomegalyCommonPortal hypertension → splenic congestion → platelet sequestration (hence the thrombocytopenia).
Hepatic encephalopathy~30–50%Ammonia plus systemic inflammation plus hyponatremia-driven astrocyte swelling. Na ≤130 confers OR 3.4 for HE.
Spider angiomata30–47%Hyperestrogenemia from impaired hepatic estrogen metabolism → cutaneous arteriolar dilation. Specificity ~95%.
AsterixisWith overt HEImpaired cortical inhibition of postural motor neurons — a negative myoclonus, i.e. a lapse in tone rather than a contraction.
Palmar erythema~23%Same hyperestrogenic vasodilatory mechanism as spider angiomata.
Caput medusaeUncommonRecanalized umbilical vein — a portosystemic collateral decompressing the portal system through the anterior abdominal wall.

Provenance, stated honestly: cited figures (ascites, hyponatremia 49%/22%, spider angiomata 30–47%, palmar erythema 23%) come from AASLD 2021 and cirrhosis physical-exam literature. Frequencies marked "~" or "common" are typical-range estimates for decompensated cirrhosis with HRS — precise symptom-level frequencies specifically in HRS-AKI are not well characterized in the published literature, and are not presented here as cohort-derived. Overall, the sensitivity of physical findings in cirrhosis ranges from 31% to 96% depending on the sign: the exam alone neither rules in nor rules out.

Tense ascites with visible dilated superficial abdominal wall veins and scattered spider angiomata. This is the substrate — every HRS patient looks like this before the creatinine ever moves.

The differential — AKI in cirrhosis

AASLD 2021, verbatim: "In large studies, AKI is attributed to hypovolemia (27%–50% of all cases), HRS-AKI (15%–43%), and ATN (14%–35%)." A large prospective North American cohort of 161 hospitalized patients with decompensated cirrhosis split almost evenly: prerenal 35%, HRS 34%, ATN 30%.

CauseShareWhat gives it away
Prerenal / hypovolemic27–50%GI losses, over-diuresis, bleeding, poor intake, large-volume tap without albumin. Defining feature: it responds to volume.
HRS-AKI15–43%Prerenal physiology that does not respond to volume. Bland sediment, urine Na typically <10 mEq/L.
Acute tubular necrosis14–35%Usually after septic or hypovolemic shock; less often a nephrotoxin. Muddy-brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cell casts.
Bile cast nephropathyUnder-recognizedFound in 44.8% (57/127) of post-mortem renal biopsies in HRS-related AKI — and 74.4% in ACLF vs 29.7% without. Independent predictors: direct bilirubin and presence of ACLF. Intratubular, predominantly distal bile casts. Diagnosis formally requires biopsy.
Abdominal compartment syndromeSee numbersTense ascites raises renal venous pressure and destroys the transrenal perfusion gradient. In critically ill cirrhotics, intra-abdominal hypertension prevalence 82.1%, ACS 23.2%; RRT needed in 38.9% with ACS vs 1.2% with normal pressure. ACS = sustained intra-abdominal pressure >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction. Therapeutic paracentesis is both the test and the treatment.
Glomerular diseaseUncommonIgA nephropathy in alcohol-associated cirrhosis; membranous or membranoproliferative GN in HBV/HCV cirrhosis (cryoglobulinemic MPGN is the classic HCV association). Suspect with proteinuria and/or hematuria.
Post-renal obstructionUncommonRare in cirrhosis, but must still be excluded — that is what the mandatory renal ultrasound is for.
Why you will see conflicting numbers. EASL 2018 states prerenal AKI accounts for "approximately 68%" of cases — because EASL counts HRS within "prerenal." AASLD separates them. Both are right; they are drawing the boundary in different places.
Urine sediment is free, fast, and the single most discriminating bedside test. Panel b shows a muddy-brown granular cast — the signature of ATN, and the finding that should stop you from calling it HRS. HRS gives a bland sediment.
Mohsenin V., CC BY 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons, RTE cast, muddy granular cast, WBC cast and RBC cast in urine.jpg
Scleral icterus. In a deeply jaundiced patient with AKI, look at the sediment yourself for green-brown bile-stained casts — bile cast nephropathy is common in ACLF and will not respond to terlipressin.
Sheila J. Toro, CC BY 4.0 — Wikimedia Commons, Scleral Icterus.jpg
🧪

Lab interpretation — why each number moves

Creatinine — and why it systematically underestimates renal dysfunction here

This is the highest-yield concept in the topic. Four independent mechanisms all push creatinine down in cirrhosis:

  1. Reduced hepatic creatine synthesis. Creatine, creatinine's precursor, is made mainly in the liver — production falls by roughly half in cirrhosis.
  2. Sarcopenia. Creatinine generation is proportional to muscle mass, and sarcopenia is present in 14–55% of patients with cirrhosis.
  3. Expanded volume of distribution. Ascites and total-body water overload dilute it.
  4. Bilirubin interference with Jaffe-method assays falsely lowers the measured value (described above a bilirubin of roughly 2.3 mg/dL). Enzymatic assays are less affected — know which one your lab runs, because it changes both the creatinine and the MELD.
A creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL in a sarcopenic cirrhotic woman may represent a GFR under 40 mL/min. Every creatinine-based eGFR equation overestimates GFR in cirrhosis. EASL 2018 puts it directly: "even a mild increase in SCr should be considered since it may underlie a marked decrease of GFR." This matters because terlipressin response falls from 49.2% at baseline creatinine <3 mg/dL to 9.1% at ≥5 mg/dL — the lag between true GFR loss and an alarming creatinine is exactly the window in which the drug still works.
TestDirection in HRSMechanism & what confounds it
Urine sodiumLow, typically <10 mEq/LMaximal aldosterone- and sympathetically-driven reabsorption. Any diuretic exposure invalidates it.
FENa<1%, often <0.2%Cannot separate HRS from true prerenal AKI — the sodium-avid physiology is identical. Published data: FENa and FEUrea were "unable to differentiate between prerenal AKI and HRS-AKI (AUC <70%)." ADQI/ICA 2024 notes FENa <1% is common in cirrhosis even without AKI. What it is good for: a high FENa (>2%) argues against both and for ATN. A low FENa tells you almost nothing.
Urine osmolalityHigh (concentrated)Isosthenuric (~300 mOsm/kg) in ATN. Same limitation — does not separate HRS from prerenal. No guideline cutoff exists; do not invent one.
Urinalysis / sedimentBlandAASLD uses proteinuria >500 mg/day and >50 RBC/hpf as the structural-injury exclusions. Caveats: sediment is hard to read at high bilirubin with real interobserver variability, and EASL warns that absent proteinuria/hematuria does not rule out renal lesions.
Urine NGALIntermediateThe best available discriminator. AASLD: best cutoffs are 365 ng/mL (ELISA) and 220 µg/g creatinine (particle-enhanced turbidimetry); best measured on day 3. Median values: ATN 344 µg/g, HRS 110 µg/g, prerenal 45 µg/g — HRS sits in the middle. ADQI/ICA 2024 adds a response signal: terlipressin response 70% if NGAL <220 µg/g vs 33% if above. Not widely available — never delay treatment for it.
Cystatin CMore accurate than creatinineIndependent of muscle mass and unaffected by bilirubin. But it is not in MELD, not in the ICA criteria, and has no guideline-endorsed cutoff for diagnosing HRS.
Serum sodiumLowNon-osmotic ADH. Grading: mild 126–135, moderate 120–125, severe <120 mEq/L. Na ≤130 → OR 3.4 for HE, 3.5 for HRS, 2.4 for SBP.
PotassiumEither wayHigh with aldosterone antagonists, ACE inhibitors, or falling GFR (>5.5); low with loop diuretics and hyperaldosteronism (<3.5).
BilirubinHighNot just a marker — mechanistically drives bile-salt tubular toxicity and bile cast nephropathy, and >10 mg/dL predicts terlipressin non-response.
INRProlongedReduced synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, X. This does not mean "auto-anticoagulated" — protein C, protein S and antithrombin fall in parallel. Cirrhosis is a rebalanced, not a hypocoagulable, state. Do not transfuse plasma to "correct" it before a tap.
AlbuminLowReduced synthesis plus dilution plus capillary leak. Simultaneously a MELD 3.0 variable and a therapy.
PlateletsLowSplenic sequestration from portal hypertension plus reduced thrombopoietin.
AmmoniaOften highNot for diagnosis or titration. AASLD HE guidance: "high blood-ammonia levels alone do not add any diagnostic, staging, or prognostic value." A normal ammonia in suspected overt HE should prompt diagnostic re-evaluation. Titrate lactulose to bowel movements and mental status, never to an ammonia level.

Ascitic fluid — the SAAG and SBP

SAAG = serum albumin − ascitic albumin, from simultaneous samples.

SAAGMeaningCauses
≥1.1 g/dLPortal hypertension present — accuracy ~97%Cirrhosis; massive liver metastases; ascites from liver involvement in right heart failure
<1.1 g/dLPortal hypertension excludedPeritoneal carcinomatosis; tuberculous peritonitis; other

Second axis — ascitic total protein. A high ascitic protein (>2.5 g/dL) with a high SAAG points to a post-sinusoidal or cardiac cause rather than cirrhosis. A low ascitic protein (<1.5 g/dL) is the SBP-prophylaxis threshold.

SBP = ascitic PMN ≥250/mm³. The same threshold defines spontaneous bacterial empyema in pleural fluid — but do not place a chest tube for it. Bacterascites (PMN <250 with a positive culture and no signs of infection): do not treat, repeat the tap. Reassess with a repeat tap at 48 hours: a fall in PMN of <25% means non-response — broaden antibiotics and look for secondary peritonitis. Treat for 5–7 days.

Imaging — what to order, when, and what it must show

StudyWhat it must show / thresholdWhen
Renal ultrasoundNormal size and echogenicity, no hydronephrosis. An abnormal renal ultrasound is an exclusion criterion for HRS. Worry about: small echogenic kidneys (chronic disease), asymmetry (vascular), hydronephrosis (post-renal), increased cortical echogenicity (parenchymal disease)Every patient with AKI and cirrhosis — mandatory to make the diagnosis
Abdominal US with DopplerPortal vein patency (thrombosis), flow direction (hepatofugal), splenomegaly, collaterals, ascites volume, HCC surveillanceInitial workup of ascites and of new-onset ascites
Echocardiography2019 Cirrhotic Cardiomyopathy Consortium criteria — systolic: LVEF ≤50% or absolute global longitudinal strain <18%; diastolic: ≥3 of E/e′ ≥15, septal e′ <7 cm/s, TR velocity >2.8 m/s, LAVI >34 mL/m²New-onset ascites (to exclude cardiac ascites), pre-TIPS, pre-transplant, or suspected cirrhotic cardiomyopathy
Doppler renal resistive indexReported thresholds vary (RI ≥0.7 and ≥0.77 both used); mean RI ~0.77 in cirrhosis vs ~0.61 in healthy controls. An independent predictor of subsequent HRS in cohort studiesInvestigational and prognostic only. Not validated as a diagnostic test and not in any guideline's HRS criteria — do not use an RI cutoff to make the diagnosis
IVC / POCUS volume assessment—ADQI/ICA 2024 is explicitly cautious: POCUS is "prone to interobserver variability and is challenging to use in patients with significant ascites." Do not teach IVC collapsibility as reliable in tense ascites — the ascites mechanically alters IVC dynamics
Central venous pressureAASLD targets CVP 4–10 mmHg when albumin accompanies norepinephrineEASL 2018 is skeptical that CVP measures volume responsiveness, but allows it "may be helpful to prevent circulatory overload." Use it as a ceiling, not a target
Chest radiographBaseline before albumin/terlipressin; then watch for new edemaAdmission, then daily while on albumin + terlipressin
ElastographyEstablishes or excludes cirrhosis and portal hypertensionNew-onset ascites workup. No role in diagnosing HRS itself
Diagnostic paracentesis. Every cirrhotic with ascites admitted for any reason gets one — ideally within 12 hours. Early paracentesis is associated with lower in-hospital mortality (OR 0.51 within 12 h). Coagulopathy is not a contraindication and clotting factors should not be transfused to "cover" it.
BruceBlaus, CC BY 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons, Blausen 0004 AbdominalParacentesis.png
Esophageal varices on endoscopy — the other consequence of the same portal hypertension that drives HRS. Variceal bleeding is a classic HRS precipitant, and it is why the beta-blocker you hold today must be reconsidered once the circulation recovers.

Who is at risk, and when to worry

🔍

The framing that matters

Every clinic visit for a patient with cirrhotic ascites is an HRS-prevention visit. By the time HRS is diagnosable, the patient is inpatient and the odds are poor. What you control in clinic is the list of things that precipitate it: infection, over-diuresis, large-volume taps without albumin, NSAIDs, GI bleeding, and untreated portal hypertension.

Risk anchorNumber
Ascites develops in compensated cirrhosis5–10% per year. Its onset drops 5-year survival from 80% to 30%
Probability of developing HRS once ascites is present (non-azotemic)18% at 1 year, 39% at 5 years (Ginès 1993)
AKI in hospitalized decompensated cirrhosis27–53%; 30-day mortality with AKI 29–44%
Hyponatremia Na ≤130OR 3.5 for developing HRS
The highest-yield thing you can do in clinic is not a drug — it is checking that the patient is not being quietly over-diuresed. The peritoneum can only reabsorb about 500 mL/day. Weight loss beyond 0.5 kg/day without edema, or 1 kg/day with edema, contracts plasma volume and is a leading iatrogenic cause of HRS.

Outpatient labs and imaging

BMP (Cr, Na, K)Within 1–2 weeks of any diuretic dose change; every 1–3 months when stable. AASLD requires that "body weight and serum creatinine and sodium should be regularly monitored" but sets no numeric interval — the intervals here are conventional practice.Routine

Class A = 5–6 points, B = 7–9, C = 10–15. Deliberately omitted: the familiar Child-Pugh 1- and 2-year survival table (100/85, 81/57, 45/35) is quoted everywhere but traces to no identifiable primary publication and is not from Pugh 1973 (which reported operative mortality). The class and its consequences are given instead. Note also that INR bands vary slightly between sources — MDCalc uses <1.7 / 1.7–2.3 / >2.3, as here; some references use 2.2 as the upper cut.

MELD 3.0 and MELD-Na are not reimplemented here on purpose. They are continuous logarithmic formulas with sex and interaction terms; a transcription error would be silent and dangerous. Use MDCalc — MELD 3.0 or MDCalc — MELD-Na. What to remember: MELD 3.0 became the US allocation score on 13 July 2023, and it caps creatinine at 3.0 mg/dL partly because creatinine underestimates renal dysfunction in the sarcopenic and malnourished — the same lie described in the lab section.

Chronic management of ascites

💊

Stepwise therapy — first-line → escalation

1
Sodium restriction + diuretics
The anchor. Sodium restriction without diuretics rarely works; diuretics without sodium restriction rarely work either.
▾
Cirrhotic ascites is a hyperaldosteronism state — the whole point of the cascade is avid distal sodium reabsorption. That is why the aldosterone antagonist is the workhorse here and the loop diuretic is the adjunct, which is the reverse of how you treat heart failure.

Diet: moderate sodium restriction to 2 g (90 mmol) per day. Fluid restriction is not needed unless sodium is ≤125 mmol/L. Do not over-restrict — AASLD explicitly warns to guard against precipitating malnutrition and sarcopenia, which are themselves mortality risks and which mask renal dysfunction by lowering creatinine.

DrugStartTitrationMaxWhy it worksIf intolerant
Spironolactone100 mg/dayIncrease stepwise, no sooner than every 72 hours — the long half-life means the full effect of a change is not visible for up to 3 days400 mg/dayAldosterone-receptor antagonist — blocks the exact hormone driving distal Na⁺ retentionPainful gynecomastia → switch to eplerenone ~50 mg or amiloride ~10 mg (AASLD's stated equivalents for spironolactone 100 mg). Hyperkalemia >5.5 → reduce dose
Furosemide40 mg/dayIncrease with the spironolactone, keeping the 100:40 ratio — 100/40 → 200/80 → 300/120 → 400/160160 mg/day — the generally accepted threshold defining medical refractorinessLoop diuretic — adds proximal natriuresis the aldosterone antagonist cannot achieve aloneTorsemide or bumetanide "may improve natriuresis in patients with a suboptimal response to furosemide" (AASLD gives no specific dose for either). Sulfa allergy → ethacrynic acid is the non-sulfonamide loop

Sourcing note: the starting doses, titration interval and maxima above are verbatim AASLD 2021. The 100:40 ratio is universal practice and the usual rationale — that spironolactone's potassium-sparing effect offsets furosemide's potassium-wasting, keeping the patient normokalemic — is standard teaching rather than a quoted AASLD sentence. Conventional loop equivalences (furosemide 40 mg ≈ torsemide 20 mg ≈ bumetanide 1 mg) are pharmacology teaching, not stated in this guideline.

Start with one drug or two? AASLD: for a first episode of ascites, an aldosterone antagonist alone gives an adequate response with fewer side effects; long-standing ascites responds better to combination therapy. In CKD, use higher loop doses and lower aldosterone-antagonist doses.
The single most important safety number in outpatient cirrhosis. The peritoneum reabsorbs only ~500 mL/day. In a patient without peripheral edema, weight loss exceeding 0.5 kg/day contracts plasma volume and predisposes to renal failure and hyponatremia. With edema, up to 1 kg/day is tolerated. Adverse effects of diuretics occur in 20–40% of patients with cirrhosis and ascites.

When ascites is controlled, taper to the lowest dose that maintains minimal or no ascites — do not leave a patient on 400/160 indefinitely.

Muscle cramps are common and genuinely reduce quality of life. AASLD: albumin 20–40 g/week, or baclofen 10 mg/day, increasing by 10 mg/day weekly, up to 30 mg/day, may be considered for severe cramps.

2
Large-volume paracentesis with albumin
First-line once ascites is refractory — and the albumin is not optional.
▾

Refractory ascites = no response to maximum diuretic doses (typically 400 mg spironolactone + 160 mg furosemide), or the development of diuretic complications. AASLD: "LVP is the first-line treatment for RA."

SituationAlbumin
Tap of >5 L6–8 g per liter removed. After 5 L ≈ 40 g; after 8 L ≈ 64 g
Tap of <5 L in a stable patientGenerally not required — smaller taps are not associated with significant hemodynamic change
Smaller tap but SBP <90 mmHg, Na <130 mmol/L, or AKIGive albumin anyway — AASLD says it "should be strongly considered"

Why: removing large volumes abruptly drops intra-abdominal pressure, the splanchnic bed expands further, and effective arterial volume falls — post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction (PPCD), which manifests as renal impairment including HRS, dilutional hyponatremia, encephalopathy and death. Ginès 1996 (N=289) found PPCD in 18.5% with albumin vs 34.4% with dextran 70 and 37.8% with polygeline, and PPCD shortened survival (9.3 vs 16.9 months). The risk rises with >8 L removed in a single session.

3
TIPS, and referral for transplant
The only definitive answers to portal hypertension.
▾

TIPS controls refractory ascites better than repeated LVP and carries a survival advantage in well-selected patients — especially younger patients with lower MELD, smaller-diameter covered stents, and a complete response. But note the context boundary: TIPS is not recommended once HRS-AKI has developed (AASLD: "insufficient information").

Transplant referral triggers (AASLD guidance statements):

  • Referral for transplant evaluation "should be considered in patients with grade 2 or 3 ascites" — that is, any clinically detectable ascites
  • "LT should be considered in patients with refractory ascites"
  • "All patients with cirrhosis and AKI should be considered for urgent LT evaluation"

AASLD uses MELD >18 as an example threshold at which liver dysfunction should prompt transplant referral rather than TIPS, and notes patients with refractory ascites are disadvantaged by MELD-based allocation — carrying an additional mortality risk equivalent to 4.5 MELD points, particularly when MELD is <21.

🛡️

Beta-blockers & SBP prophylaxis — the two prevention levers

Nonselective beta-blockers — full dose ladders

Doses from the AASLD 2024 Practice Guidance on portal hypertension and varices (Kaplan et al., Hepatology 2024;79:1180–1211). Carvedilol is now the preferred agent — note that EASL 2018's statement that carvedilol "cannot be recommended" is obsolete, superseded by Baveno VII (2022) and AASLD 2024.

DrugStartTitrationMaxGoal
Carvedilol
preferred		6.25 mg once dailyIncrease to 6.25 mg twice daily after 3 days12.5 mg/day (higher doses only for non-hepatic indications)No heart-rate goal; keep SBP ≥90 mmHg
Propranolol20–40 mg twice dailyIncrease every 2–3 days until goal320 mg/day without ascites; 160 mg/day with ascitesHR 55–60 bpm if tolerated; SBP ≥90 mmHg
Nadolol20–40 mg at bedtimeAs above160 mg/day without ascites; 80 mg/day with ascitesAs above

Lower starting doses are more appropriate in Child-Pugh B and C. If carvedilol drops the pressure too far even at low dose, AASLD suggests switching to propranolol or nadolol, which affect arterial pressure less. Continue indefinitely, or until TIPS or transplant.

The window hypothesis — when to hold. Beta-blockers help while portal hypertension is the problem and harm once the circulation decompensates. Hold for: SBP <90 mmHg · MAP <65 mmHg · serum Na <130 mmol/L · creatinine >1.5 mg/dL or any AKI · SBP (the infection) with hypotension. Reintroduce when circulatory dysfunction improves — and if you stop permanently, AASLD says that should prompt endoscopic evaluation for high-risk varices needing band ligation. Never stopping is a mistake; never restarting is the more common one.

SBP prophylaxis — the intervention that most reduces HRS

IndicationCriteriaRegimen
Secondary (prior SBP)Any patient who has recovered from an episode of SBPLong-term daily norfloxacin; where unavailable — which includes the entire United States, where norfloxacin is no longer marketed — oral ciprofloxacin is acceptable. Conventional doses are norfloxacin 400 mg daily, ciprofloxacin 500 mg daily, or TMP-SMX DS daily; AASLD's guidance statement does not itself specify the milligram dose
PrimaryAscitic fluid protein <1.5 g/dL plus either renal dysfunction (creatinine >1.2 mg/dL, BUN >25 mg/dL, or Na <130 mEq/L) or liver failure (Child-Pugh >9 with bilirubin >3 mg/dL)Same agents. AASLD stresses the evidence is not strong, is restricted to very advanced cirrhosis, and must be individualized against fluoroquinolone safety warnings from the FDA and EMA
After upper GI bleedingAny cirrhotic with upper GI hemorrhageIV ceftriaxone 1 g every 24 hours, for a maximum of 7 days
This is the cleanest "prevention beats treatment" citation in hepatology. Fernández 2007 randomized cirrhotics meeting exactly the primary-prophylaxis criteria above to norfloxacin 400 mg/day or placebo: 1-year SBP fell from 61% to 7% (P<0.001), 1-year HRS from 41% to 28% (P=0.02), and 3-month survival rose from 62% to 94% (P=0.003). No drug in the inpatient half of this guide comes close to that effect size.
Do not start scheduled outpatient albumin. The evidence is genuinely split — ANSWER (N=431) gave 40 g twice weekly for 2 weeks then weekly for 18 months and found 18-month survival 77% vs 66%, a 38% reduction in mortality hazard; MACHT (2018, 196 randomized, transplant-listed patients) gave 40 g every 15 days plus midodrine 15–30 mg/day and found no difference in complications or death. AASLD's position is explicit: "At present, no recommendation can be made for its use in routine clinical practice."

WeightDaily at home, reviewed every visitLoss >0.5 kg/day (no edema) or >1 kg/day (edema) → reduce diuretics
Creatinine + sodiumWithin 1–2 weeks of a dose change; every 1–3 months stableCr rise ≥0.3 mg/dL → stop diuretics, evaluate for AKI. Na <130 → hold NSBB, restrict fluid

AASLD requires regular monitoring of weight, creatinine and sodium but does not specify a numeric interval — the intervals above are conventional practice, labeled as such.

Prevent

USPSTF A/B & the never-list

🛡️

Grade A & B screening relevant to this population

GradeRecommendationPopulationYear
BScreening for hepatitis C virus infectionAdults aged 18 to 79 years2020
BScreening for hepatitis B virus infectionNon-pregnant adolescents and adults at increased risk2020
BScreening for unhealthy alcohol use + brief behavioral counselingAdults 18 years or older, including pregnant persons2018
Note what these three have in common: they target the etiologies of cirrhosis — hepatitis C, hepatitis B, and alcohol. USPSTF screening in this population is, quite literally, primary prevention of hepatorenal syndrome. The 2020 HCV recommendation replaced the old 1945–1965 birth-cohort approach; do not teach birth-cohort-only screening.

A 2025 USPSTF draft update on unhealthy alcohol use proposed retaining Grade B for adults and adding an I statement for adolescents; the 2018 statement remains the current final recommendation.

Vaccination in chronic liver disease conventionally includes hepatitis A, hepatitis B, annual influenza, pneumococcal and COVID-19. ACIP pneumococcal age and product thresholds changed in 2024–2025 — check the current CDC/ACIP adult schedule rather than relying on this page for the specific product or age.

The clinic never-list. AASLD guidance statements, verbatim: "Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor blockers should be avoided in patients with cirrhosis and ascites" and "Aminoglycosides should be avoided whenever possible." Also named: α₁-adrenergic blockers and dipyridamole. Add: unmonitored diuretics, large-volume paracentesis without albumin, and ongoing alcohol use. IV contrast is not absolutely contraindicated but demands caution with impaired renal function.
Escalate

Red flags → ED / admission

🚑

Specific findings that mean "not in clinic"

Red flagThreshold
Creatinine rise≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 h, or ≥50% from baseline — this is AKI by ICA criteria
Absolute creatinine with ascites≥1.5 mg/dL — AKI stage 1B, prognostically like stage 2–3
Fever, abdominal pain, or any unexplained deteriorationNeeds a diagnostic paracentesis; SBP if PMN ≥250/mm³
HyponatremiaNa <125 mmol/L
HypotensionSBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg
New or worsening encephalopathyAny grade change; grade 3–4 = brain failure, go to ED
Organ-failure thresholdsBilirubin ≥12 mg/dL, INR ≥2.5, creatinine ≥2 mg/dL
OliguriaIndependently associated with poor prognosis
Over-diuresisWeight loss >0.5 kg/day without edema or >1 kg/day with edema
GI bleedingAny — a classic HRS precipitant
Any hospital admission in a patient with ascites — for any reason at all — warrants a diagnostic paracentesis, even if they are completely asymptomatic. AASLD is unambiguous about this, and it is the single most commonly skipped order in the entire disease.
🛏️ Wards — the patient is admitted and the creatinine is climbing
Admit

Who to admit, and where

📋

Admission triggers — with numbers

AASLD 2021 is direct about the tempo: "Once AKI is diagnosed, it should be treated as soon as possible, and if the patient has concomitant complications such as severe hepatic encephalopathy or multiorgan failure or requires RRT, management in an intensive or intermediate care unit should be considered."

Admit any cirrhotic with ascites who has:

  • ICA-AKI stage 1B or higher — i.e. a qualifying creatinine rise with an absolute creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL; and effectively any stage 2 or 3
  • New or worsening ascites with a creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL
  • Serum sodium ≤130 mEq/L. AASLD reports Na ≤130 carries an odds ratio of 3.5 for developing HRS (and 3.4 for hepatic encephalopathy, 2.4 for SBP), with worse in-hospital and waitlist mortality
  • Any suspicion of SBP — abdominal pain, fever, new encephalopathy, AKI, or simply unexplained decompensation
  • GI bleeding in a cirrhotic — a classic HRS precipitant
  • HE grade ≥2 (monitored bed); grade 3–4 → ICU for airway
  • MAP <65 mmHg, rising lactate, or suspected infection
Straight to ICU, not the floor, for any of: HE grade 3–4 · shock requiring vasopressors · PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤200 or SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤214 · need for RRT · ACLF grade 2–3 (≥2 organ failures) · GI bleeding with hemodynamic instability.
🧮

ICA-AKI stage calculator

Staging drives everything downstream. Enter the baseline creatinine (a stable value from the previous 3 months) and the current value.

Also true?
On renal replacement therapy
—

Orders

Admission order set

🧪

Labs, imaging, monitoring — and what each one changes

BMPOn arrival, then q12h × 48 h, then q24h minimum while on a vasoconstrictor. The creatinine trajectory is the therapeutic endpoint and the dosing algorithm.Admit
LFTs, bilirubin, INR, albuminDaily initially. Bilirubin >10 mg/dL predicts terlipressin non-response; INR + bilirubin + creatinine give you a daily MELD.Admit
CBC, lactate, VBG/ABG, Mg/Phos/CapH <7.2 is an RRT trigger. Lactate flags occult sepsis, though cirrhotics clear lactate poorly at baseline.Admit
Urine Na, urine Cr, urine protein, microscopy with sedimentProteinuria >500 mg/day or >50 RBC/hpf argues against HRS. Look at the sediment yourself: granular/muddy-brown casts → ATN; green-brown bile-stained casts → bile cast nephropathy.Admit
Cultures ×3 sitesBlood ×2, urine, and ascitic fluid inoculated into blood-culture bottles at the bedside (bedside inoculation roughly doubles yield).Admit
Diagnostic paracentesisWithin 12 hours. This is the highest-yield order on the list. Send cell count with differential, total protein, albumin (for SAAG), Gram stain, cultures. SBP = ascitic PMN ≥250/mm³. Coagulopathy is not a contraindication — do not transfuse platelets or plasma to "cover" it.≤12 h
Renal ultrasound with DopplerMandatory — excludes obstruction and satisfies the "no structural injury" criterion. Also sizes the kidneys and reads echogenicity for underlying CKD.Admit
Chest radiographGet a baseline before any albumin load or terlipressin — volume overload and respiratory failure are the therapy-limiting toxicities, and you will want something to compare to on day 4.Admit
EchocardiogramIf TIPS is contemplated or cirrhotic cardiomyopathy is suspected (blunted contractile reserve changes how much volume they tolerate).If indicated
Urinary NGALWhere available, helps separate ATN from HRS. AASLD Table 12 cutoffs: 365 ng/mL (Belcher 2014, AUROC 0.78) and 220 µg/g creatinine (Huelin 2019, AUROC 0.87, Sn/Sp 88/85). Do not delay treatment waiting for it.Optional
Telemetry + continuous pulse oximetryContinuous pulse oximetry is an FDA-label requirement for terlipressin, not a nicety. Telemetry for arrhythmia and ischemia surveillance on any vasoconstrictor.Admit
Strict I/O + daily standing weightsSame scale, same time each day. Net gain >1–2 kg/day means hold albumin and reassess.Admit
Foley catheter — NOAASLD 2021 states plainly: "Indwelling bladder catheterization should be avoided." Catheter-associated infection is a direct HRS precipitant in a patient whose whole prognosis turns on avoiding infection. Use a condom catheter, weighed pads, a urinal with strict collection, or intermittent straight cath. Urine volume still matters — oliguria predicts poor outcome — so solve it without the Foley.Avoid
Avoid iodinated contrast — but for the right reason. Modern prospective data put contrast nephrotoxicity in cirrhosis close to baseline risk, and AASLD calls for caution rather than prohibition. The reason to avoid it here is diagnostic: recent contrast is an explicit exclusion in the HRS-AKI criteria, so a contrast study on hospital day 1 can cost you the diagnosis.

The stop orders — write these before you write anything else

HoldWhy
All diuretics — furosemide, spironolactone, torsemide, metolazoneAASLD: "Diuretics should be stopped after the diagnosis of AKI." They deepen the effective-volume deficit that is causing the problem.
NSAIDs (including home ibuprofen/naproxen, ketorolac)Remove prostaglandin-mediated afferent vasodilation — the last defense holding GFR up. Can convert compensated cirrhosis to anuric HRS in a day.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aliskirenBlock efferent constriction and drop systemic pressure in a patient who is already vasoplegic.
Aminoglycosides; vancomycin if avoidable; iodinated contrastAminoglycosides cause direct tubular toxicity. Contrast is primarily a diagnostic problem — recent exposure is an explicit exclusion in the criteria.
Nonselective beta-blockersSee the window discussion below — hold, but plan to restart.
SGLT2 inhibitorsVolume depletion and euglycemic DKA risk.
Over-titrated lactulose — target 2–3 soft stools/dayRunaway lactulose causes profound hypovolemic, hypernatremic losses that both cause and mimic HRS.
The nonselective beta-blocker call is nuanced — hold, do not abandon. AASLD 2021: NSBBs are "not necessarily contraindicated" in refractory ascites, but caution applies with SBP <90 mmHg, serum Na <130 mmol/L, or creatinine >1.5 mg/dL; for SBP specifically, "NSBBs should be temporarily held in patients with SBP who develop hypotension (MAP <65 mm Hg) or AKI." Critically, they "might be reintroduced if circulatory dysfunction improves." This is the window hypothesis: beta-blockers help in earlier cirrhosis and harm once circulatory failure supervenes. The common error is not holding the drug — it is never restarting it, leaving the patient unprotected from variceal bleeding.
Treat

The management ladder

🧭

The whole algorithm on one page

Diagnosis and treatment of AKI in cirrhosis. Criteria per AASLD 2021 Table 11 with the ADQI/ICA 2024 consensus revisions; drug sequencing per the AASLD 2021 guidance statement.
💊

Stepwise therapy — first-line → escalation

1
Remove the insult + the volume challenge
Diagnostic and therapeutic at the same time — you cannot call it HRS until this fails.
▾
Hyperoncotic albumin pulls interstitial fluid back into the arterial compartment, raising the effective volume the baroreceptors sense, which switches off RAAS/SNS/ADH and releases the renal arteriole. If the AKI was simply hypovolemic, this alone fixes it — which is exactly why it doubles as the diagnostic test.
AgentStartTitrationTarget / maxWhy it worksCautions
Albumin 25%1 g/kg/day IVFixed dose — given across the day, not as a single bolus2 consecutive days, then reassess. Commonly capped at 100 g/dayOncotic expansion + binds NO, endotoxin, bilirubin and bile acids; stabilizes endotheliumStop for new hypoxemia, crackles, rising JVP, worsening CXR

Sourcing note: the 1 g/kg/day × 2 days comes verbatim from AASLD 2021 Table 11. The 100 g/day ceiling is practice/EASL convention and is not stated in AASLD 2021 — use it as a sensible cap, not as a guideline-mandated number.

Practical: 25% albumin comes in 50 mL (12.5 g) and 100 mL (25 g) bottles. An 80 kg patient needs 80 g/day ≈ three 100 mL bottles plus one 50 mL bottle, spread through the day.

Simultaneously: hold all diuretics, remove nephrotoxins, treat any infection, control any bleeding. In SBP, give the disease-specific albumin regimen instead: 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 (Sort 1999; endorsed by AASLD 2021).

Albumin is a drug, not a benign volume expander. ATTIRE (N=777) targeted albumin to a serum level ≥30 g/L in hospitalized decompensated cirrhotics and found no benefit (29.7% vs 30.2%, adjusted OR 0.98) with more severe or life-threatening serious adverse events, driven by pulmonary edema and fluid overload. Over-albuminizing a patient today also makes them ineligible for terlipressin tomorrow, because volume overload is a boxed-warning risk factor.
2
Vasoconstrictor + albumin — the core therapy
Terlipressin first-line; norepinephrine if unavailable; midodrine + octreotide only if neither.
▾

AASLD 2021 guidance statement, verbatim: "The treatment of choice for HRS-AKI is vasoconstrictor drugs in combination with albumin. The preferred drug is terlipressin, administered either as IV bolus or continuous IV infusion. In settings where terlipressin is not available, norepinephrine should be given. If neither can be administered, a trial of oral midodrine (5 to 15 mg per os every 8 hours) in combination with octreotide (100 to 200 μg every 8 hours or 50 μg/hour IV) may be considered, yet the efficacy is low."

Overall response to vasoconstrictor + albumin across RCTs and meta-analyses is 20–80%, averaging about 50% (AASLD 2021). Full dose ladders for every agent are in the next module.

All three regimens do the same thing by different receptors: constrict the dilated splanchnic bed, restore effective arterial volume, and switch off the renal vasoconstriction. Terlipressin hits V1a receptors, which are concentrated on splanchnic vessels — that selectivity is why it is the most effective and why it spares the kidney. Norepinephrine uses α1, less selectively. Midodrine (α1) plus octreotide (blocks splanchnic vasodilator peptides) is the weakest because midodrine is simply a far less potent vasoconstrictor.
3
Non-response — RRT, TIPS, transplant, or goals of care
Every path here forks on one question: is this patient a transplant candidate?
▾

If creatinine remains at or above the pretreatment level for 4 days at maximum tolerated dose, therapy may be discontinued (AASLD 2021). What happens next depends entirely on transplant candidacy:

  • Transplant candidate → RRT as a bridge; urgent transplant evaluation; ICU as needed. Full detail in the ICU context.
  • Not a candidate → AASLD: "Initiation of RRT in patients who are not candidates for LT must be made with a clear endpoint in mind," and mortality is "extremely high in patients not listed for LT who receive RRT." If you cannot state the endpoint out loud, the honest next step is a goals-of-care conversation, not a dialysis catheter.

TIPS is not the answer here. AASLD 2021, verbatim: "TIPS is not recommended in patients with AKI-HRS because of insufficient information." The ongoing Liver-HERO RCT (TIPS vs terlipressin + albumin, primary endpoint 12-month transplant-free survival) is designed to settle this; results were not published as of this build.

💉

Full dose ladders — every vasoconstrictor

Terlipressin — first-line, and the only FDA-approved drug for this indication

Approved 14 September 2022 as TERLIVAZ. Note that AASLD 2021 predates the approval and states terlipressin "is not yet approved in United States" — dose off the FDA label, not off AASLD.

PhaseDoseRule
Days 1–3 (start)0.85 mg IV every 6 hoursSlow IV bolus over 2 minutes. Reconstitute each vial with 5 mL of 0.9% NaCl. Peripheral or central line — a dedicated central line is not required (the key practical advantage over norepinephrine on a ward). Flush after.
Day 4 — titration decisionAssess change in creatinine from baselineThe single branch point of the whole regimen.
→ Creatinine fell ≥30%Continue 0.85 mg q6hWorking — do not escalate.
→ Creatinine fell <30%Increase to 1.7 mg q6hThis is the maximum dose (6.8 mg/day).
→ Creatinine at or above baselineDiscontinueDo not escalate into futility.
Stop for success—Continue until 24 hours after two consecutive creatinine values ≤1.5 mg/dL taken ≥2 hours apart.
Maximum duration—14 days.

Unit trap: 1 mg terlipressin acetate = 0.85 mg terlipressin. The trials say "1 mg"; the US label says "0.85 mg". They are the same dose.

Boxed warning, verbatim: "TERLIVAZ may cause serious or fatal respiratory failure. Patients with volume overload or with ACLF Grade 3 are at increased risk. Assess oxygenation saturation (e.g., SpO₂) before initiating TERLIVAZ. Do not initiate TERLIVAZ in patients experiencing hypoxia (e.g., SpO₂ <90%) until oxygenation levels improve. Monitor patients for hypoxia using continuous pulse oximetry during treatment and discontinue TERLIVAZ if SpO₂ decreases below 90%."

In CONFIRM the median onset of serious respiratory events was 4.5 days (IQR 2–7) — days 4–5 are the danger window, which is exactly when you are also making the dose-escalation decision.
Do not start terlipressin if…Why
Creatinine >5 mg/dLLabel limitation of use: "Patients with a serum creatinine >5 mg/dL are unlikely to experience benefit." Pooled OT-0401/REVERSE reversal by baseline creatinine: <3 mg/dL = 49.2%; 3–5 = 28.0%; ≥5 = 9.1%.
SpO₂ <90% / hypoxia / worsening respiratory symptomsContraindicated on the label. Hard stop.
ACLF grade 3Boxed-warning risk factor; label says avoid. Grade 3 = ≥3 organ failures, 28-day mortality 76.7% (CANONIC).
Volume overloadBoxed-warning risk factor — correct it first.
Ongoing coronary, peripheral or mesenteric ischemiaContraindicated on the label.

Adverse reactions, CONFIRM safety population (label table): abdominal pain 19.5% vs 6.1%; nausea 16.0% vs 10.1%; respiratory failure 15.5% vs 7.1%; diarrhea 13.0% vs 7.1%; dyspnea 12.5% vs 5.1%; sepsis 5.5% vs 1.0%; ischemia-related events 4.5% vs 0%; discontinuation for adverse event 12.0% vs 5.1%.

What to monitor when you start terlipressin

  • Continuous pulse oximetry — a label requirement, and the single most important monitor
  • Continuous telemetry — bradycardia, arrhythmia, myocardial ischemia
  • Respiratory exam and CXR — watch days 2–7 hardest
  • Skin: digits, extremities, tip of the nose, abdominal wall — mottling, cyanosis, necrosis
  • Abdominal exam — pain in ~20%; mesenteric ischemia is the feared endpoint
  • Serum sodium — terlipressin can precipitate hyponatremia
  • Daily weights, strict I/O, BMP q12–24 h — the creatinine trend is the dosing algorithm
The European continuous-infusion regimen halves the adverse events — but you cannot use it in the US. AASLD 2021, verbatim: "The risk of ischemic side effects related to terlipressin may be reduced by administration of the drug in a continuous IV infusion (start dose 2 mg/day, increased every 24–48 hours up to 12 mg/day until creatinine decreases)." Cavallin 2016 (N=78) found adverse events 35.3% with infusion vs 62.2% with bolus (P<0.025) at similar efficacy and lower total daily dose. The AGA 2024 update states plainly that continuous infusion is not an approved mode of administration in the United States. Know both; use the label one.

Norepinephrine — when terlipressin is unavailable or contraindicated

AASLD 2021, verbatim: "Norepinephrine is given as continuous IV infusion, typically in an intensive care unit setting, starting at 0.5 mg/hour to achieve an increase in mean arterial pressure of at least 10 mm Hg or an increase in urine output of >200 mL/4 hours. If at least one of these goals is not achieved, the dose of norepinephrine is increased every 4 hours in increments of 0.5 mg/hour up to a maximum of 3 mg/hour. Albumin is also given to maintain a central venous pressure between 4 and 10 mm Hg."

ParameterStartTitrationMaxEndpoint
Norepinephrine0.5 mg/hour
≈ 8.3 mcg/min		+0.5 mg/hour every 4 hours3 mg/hour
≈ 50 mcg/min		MAP rise ≥10 mmHg or urine output >200 mL/4 h
Unit conversion is the dangerous part. Hepatology writes norepinephrine in mg/hour; your ICU pump is almost certainly programmed in mcg/min or mcg/kg/min. For an 80 kg patient, 0.5 mg/h ≈ 0.10 mcg/kg/min and 3 mg/h ≈ 0.63 mcg/kg/min. Convert deliberately and out loud — this is a classic transcription error.

Access: central venous access, ICU or step-down. Cost: far cheaper — Singh 2012 reported 15-day drug cost of €275 for noradrenaline vs €975 for terlipressin (P<0.05), with no difference in HRS reversal (43.4% vs 39.1%, P=0.764). Monitor: arterial line or frequent cuff MAP, telemetry, digit and limb perfusion, urine output q4h, lactate, and the infusion site — norepinephrine extravasation causes tissue necrosis, and phentolamine is the antidote.

Midodrine + octreotide — the ward-safe, least effective option

DrugStartTitrationTarget / maxWhy it worksMonitor
Midodrine7.5 mg PO TIDIncrease to 12.5 mg PO TID if no response after 48 h12.5 mg TID (Cavallin 2015); AASLD's stated range tops out at 15 mg q8hOral prodrug → desglymidodrine, a peripheral-selective α1 agonist → raises systemic vascular resistanceSupine hypertension — do not dose within 4 h of bedtime; reflex bradycardia; urinary retention; piloerection/scalp tingling
Octreotide100 mcg SC TIDIncrease to 200 mcg SC TID if no response after 48 h200 mcg SC TID, or 50 mcg/hour IVSomatostatin analogue — inhibits release of splanchnic vasodilators (glucagon, VIP), reducing splanchnic dilationHyper- or hypoglycemia, bradycardia, injection-site reactions. Essentially no independent efficacy — it is an adjunct to midodrine only
Albumin (both arms)1 g/kg on day 1—Then 20–40 g/dayAs aboveHold for volume overload

Titration target: a stable rise in MAP of at least 15 mmHg.

Why so much weaker, and why use it at all? Cavallin 2015 (RCT, N=49) found recovery of renal function in 70.4% (19/27) with terlipressin + albumin vs 28.6% (6/21) with midodrine/octreotide + albumin (P=0.01). AASLD calls it "of much lower efficacy than terlipressin." But it is ward-safe — oral plus subcutaneous, no central line, no ICU bed, no infusion pump — and it is the only regimen that can be continued at discharge. In a hospital without terlipressin on formulary and without an ICU bed, it is what AASLD sanctions as third-line.

Albumin during vasoconstrictor therapy

Albumin is not optional — every positive HRS trial used vasoconstrictor plus albumin. AASLD 2021: "In conjunction with terlipressin, albumin is infused at a dose of 1 g/kg on day 1 of therapy followed by 40–50 g/day, continued for the duration of therapy." The trial protocols and the AGA framing use 20–40 g/day. Both are cited by reputable sources; use 20–40 g/day whenever volume overload is a concern — which, given the boxed warning, is most patients.

Hold albumin for: new or worsening hypoxemia or a rising oxygen requirement · rales, orthopnea, rising JVP · worsening CXR · weight gain >1–2 kg/day · CVP >10 mmHg if you are measuring it.

✅

HRS-AKI criteria checker

Work the AASLD 2021 Table 11 criteria. All six must hold.

Cirrhosis with ascites
Meets ICA-AKI criteria
No response after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal + albumin 1 g/kg/day
Absence of shock
No recent NSAIDs / aminoglycosides / contrast
No structural injury: protein <500 mg/day, <50 RBC/hpf, normal renal US
0/6
Select the criteria that are satisfied.
Remember that the 2024 ADQI/ICA consensus explicitly dropped the mandatory 2-day albumin trial — "We recommend against systematic administration of albumin for 48 h as a requisite for the diagnosis of HRS-AKI (strong recommendation, grade D)." In a deteriorating patient with a clean urinalysis and no alternative explanation, the 48-hour rule is a guideline, not a physical law. The eTerli RCT (2024, N=70, ACLF with stage II/III AKI) started terlipressin at 12 h versus 48 h and found day-7 full AKI response 68.6% vs 31.4% (P=0.03) and 28-day mortality 40% vs 65.7% (P=0.031) — single-center and hypothesis-generating, but it is the strongest argument yet for not running the clock out on a crashing patient.
Response

Defining response & when to stop

🎯

Response definitions and stop rules

AASLD 2021, verbatim: "Response to terlipressin or norepinephrine is defined by creatinine decreases to <1.5 mg/dL or return to within 0.3 mg/dL of baseline over a maximum of 14 days. In patients whose creatinine remains at or above the pretreatment level over 4 days with the maximum tolerated doses of the vasoconstrictor, therapy may be discontinued." And: "Recurrence may occur after treatment discontinuation and should be retreated."

CategoryCriterion
Full responseCreatinine falls to within 0.3 mg/dL of baseline (resolution of the AKI)
Partial responseRegression of AKI stage, but creatinine remains >0.3 mg/dL above baseline
No responseNo regression of stage; creatinine at or above the pretreatment level
FDA-label endpoint (US)Two consecutive creatinine values ≤1.5 mg/dL at least 2 hours apart → continue 24 more hours, then stop
CONFIRM primary endpoint"Verified reversal" = two consecutive creatinine ≤1.5 mg/dL ≥2 h apart by day 14 and survival without RRT for a further 10 days

The four ways therapy ends

  • Success — 24 h after the second consecutive creatinine ≤1.5 mg/dL, ≥2 h apart
  • Futility — creatinine at or above pretreatment level for 4 days at maximum tolerated dose; or, per the label, creatinine at/above baseline on day 4 (discontinue, do not escalate)
  • Toxicity — SpO₂ <90%, any ischemic event, uncontrolled volume overload
  • The clock — 14 days maximum (AASLD and FDA label). AASLD allows that a few patients with very high pretreatment creatinine need longer, and some need prolonged therapy to prevent early recurrence — but that is an off-label, individualized decision.

Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How each comorbidity changes the course and the management

ComorbidityHow it changes the diseaseHow it changes your management
Infection / SBPThe most common precipitant. Inflammation worsens vasodilation and injures tubules directly. SBP is the classic trigger.Tap early, culture at the bedside, treat empirically. Give the SBP albumin regimen (1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3) — it reduced renal impairment from 33% to 10% and in-hospital mortality from 29% to 10% (Sort 1999). Albumin does not help in non-SBP infections.
Acute-on-chronic liver failureDefines prognosis. 28-day mortality: grade 1 22.1%, grade 2 32.0%, grade 3 76.7% (CANONIC).ACLF-3 is a terlipressin boxed-warning exclusion — use norepinephrine instead. Grade ≥2 belongs in the ICU.
Cirrhotic cardiomyopathyBlunted contractile reserve — the heart cannot raise output to rescue the falling effective volume.Limits how much albumin they tolerate; a relative contraindication to TIPS (which acutely increases preload). Get an echo if TIPS is on the table.
Chronic kidney disease / diabetesReduces the chance of renal recovery even after successful transplant; blurs the "baseline creatinine."Drives the simultaneous liver–kidney transplant conversation. Higher loop-diuretic and lower aldosterone-antagonist doses are typical.
GI bleeding / varicesClassic precipitant — hypovolemia plus a protein load plus translocation.Transfuse to a restrictive threshold. Ceftriaxone 1 g/24 h for a maximum of 7 days is the AASLD-specified prophylaxis after upper GI hemorrhage.
Hepatic encephalopathyGrade 3–4 is cerebral organ failure; the airway is at risk and aspiration follows.Intubate for grade 3–4. Titrate lactulose to 2–3 soft stools/day — over-titration causes hypovolemic losses that mimic and cause HRS.
HyponatremiaNa ≤130 carries OR 3.5 for HRS; marks advanced disease and independently predicts death.Fluid restriction (1,000 mL/day for Na 120–125); cirrhosis is a maximal-risk state for osmotic demyelination — correct chronic hyponatremia slowly.
Alcohol-associated liver diseaseThe largest single etiology in US HRS cohorts (56% in HRS-HARMONY).Ongoing use may preclude transplant candidacy — which changes whether RRT has a destination. Address it explicitly and early.
Drugs to avoid or use with real caution in HRS
  • NSAIDs — absolutely avoid. Remove the prostaglandin defense of the afferent arteriole and GFR falls off a cliff.
  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs / aliskiren — avoid. Systemic hypotension in an already vasoplegic patient.
  • Aminoglycosides — avoid. Direct tubular toxicity and an explicit diagnostic exclusion.
  • Iodinated contrast — avoid; an explicit exclusion in the criteria.
  • Diuretics — stop at the moment AKI is diagnosed.
  • Nonselective beta-blockers — hold if SBP <90, Na <130, creatinine >1.5, or MAP <65 with SBP. Restart when circulation improves.
  • Vaptans (tolvaptan) — not recommended. FDA limits treatment to 30 days with a boxed warning for hepatocellular injury; the sodium effect does not persist.
  • Benzodiazepines — worsen encephalopathy and are unpredictably cleared.
  • Metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors — hold during acute illness.
  • Terlipressin itself if SpO₂ <90%, ACLF-3, volume overload, active ischemia, or creatinine >5 mg/dL.
  • Do not use terlipressin as a diagnostic test. The AGA 2024 update advises explicitly against giving it to "see if the creatinine moves" — that exposes a patient with ATN or bile cast nephropathy to boxed-warning toxicity for no possible benefit.
Escalate

When to call the ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers — any one of these

SystemTrigger
RespiratorySpO₂ <90% on supplemental O₂, or PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤200, or SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤214
NeurologicHE grade 3–4 (West Haven) — airway at risk
CirculatoryMAP <65 mmHg requiring vasopressors, or needing norepinephrine above a ward-safe ceiling
RenalCreatinine ≥2.0 mg/dL rising despite maximal therapy, or any need for RRT
MetabolicK >6.5 mEq/L refractory, or arterial pH <7.2
HepaticBilirubin ≥12 mg/dL (liver organ failure by CLIF-C OF)
CoagulationINR ≥2.5 and/or platelets <20,000/µL
Composite≥2 organ failures = ACLF grade 2
OtherActive GI bleeding with instability · rising lactate · new septic shock
A terlipressin-treated patient with new dyspnea, hypoxemia or a new infiltrate is having the boxed-warning event until proven otherwise. Stop the drug, get a chest film, and escalate — do not simply increase the oxygen and re-round in the morning.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness criteria and where they go

Ready for discharge when all of:

  • Creatinine stable or improving for ≥48 h off IV vasoconstrictors
  • No IV albumin requirement for 24–48 h
  • Ascites controlled on a stable, tolerated diuretic regimen — restarted cautiously and only once creatinine is stable — with a 2 g (90 mmol) sodium-restricted diet
  • SBP treated to completion; secondary prophylaxis started if applicable
  • HE controlled on lactulose ± rifaximin, with a caregiver who can titrate to 2–3 stools/day
  • Serum sodium stable
  • Transplant evaluation initiated, or a documented decision that the patient is not a candidate
  • Follow-up: hepatology within 1–2 weeks, BMP within 3–7 days

Home

Full responder, independent, reliable caregiver, can attend early follow-up.

Home health

Needs nursing for weights and labs, paracentesis coordination, medication management. The realistic answer for most partial responders.

SNF

Deconditioned, cannot self-manage lactulose and diuretics, needs supervised nursing. A large fraction of HRS survivors.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Only if they can tolerate ≥3 h/day of therapy with genuine rehab potential — uncommon in decompensated cirrhosis, more relevant post-transplant.

LTAC

Prolonged ventilator weaning or ongoing intermittent hemodialysis needing more nursing than a SNF provides; typically the post-ICU non-transplant patient.

Hospice

Not a transplant candidate + no response to a maximal vasoconstrictor trial + RRT would be a bridge to nowhere.
When hospice is the right answer. HRS-AKI without transplant is a terminal diagnosis. The AASLD palliative-care guidance suggests teams "may consider using MELD >21 and Child-Pugh >12 to determine whether patients are prognostically appropriate for hospice (i.e., have estimated survival of ≤6 months)." Concretely: the patient is definitively not a transplant candidate, and HRS has not responded to maximal vasoconstrictor + albumin at 4 days, and RRT has no destination. Do not defer this conversation to the next team — palliative care should be integrated early and does not preclude disease-directed treatment.
🫀 ICU — organ support, and the question of where this is going
Admit

ICU triggers & ACLF grading

🚨

Organ failure definitions — CLIF-C OF

In cirrhosis, "sick" is defined by organ-failure counting, not by gestalt. The EASL-CLIF Consortium definitions below are what generate the ACLF grade — and the ACLF grade is what determines whether terlipressin is safe.

Organ systemFailure threshold
LiverBilirubin ≥12 mg/dL
KidneyCreatinine ≥2.0 mg/dL, or on RRT
BrainGrade III–IV hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven)
CoagulationINR ≥2.5 and/or platelets <20,000/µL
CirculationUse of vasopressors for severe arterial hypotension
RespirationPaO₂/FiO₂ ≤200 or SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤214

ACLF grade and what it costs

GradeDefinition28-day mortality90-day mortality
1Single kidney failure; or another single organ failure with HE grade I–II and/or creatinine 1.5–1.9 mg/dL; or single cerebral failure with creatinine 1.5–1.922.1%40.7%
22 organ failures32.0%52.3%
3≥3 organ failures76.7%79.1%

Mortality from CANONIC (Moreau et al., Gastroenterology 2013, N=1,343). The CLIF-C OF score assigns 1–3 per organ; the kidney subscore is creatinine <2 = 1, ≥2 to <3.5 = 2, ≥3.5 or RRT = 3.

ACLF grade 3 is the terlipressin boxed-warning exclusion — and this table is why. A 76.7% 28-day mortality is the population in which the FDA saw fatal respiratory failure. In these patients use norepinephrine, not terlipressin. Note the honest tension: Arora 2020 found terlipressin superior to norepinephrine in ACLF broadly. The reconciliation is grade — the harm signal sits at grade 3, not across all ACLF.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, targets, and what actually helps

  • Central venous access — mandatory for norepinephrine. Not required for terlipressin, which the FDA label permits through a peripheral line.
  • Arterial line — for MAP-targeted titration and frequent blood gases.
  • Continuous pulse oximetry — an FDA-label requirement whenever terlipressin is running, not a nicety.
  • CVP — AASLD does target 4–10 mmHg with albumin during norepinephrine therapy. But EASL is openly skeptical that CVP measures volume responsiveness, allowing only that it "may be helpful to prevent circulatory overload." Treat CVP as a ceiling you must not exceed, not as a resuscitation target.
  • POCUS — useful for lung B-lines, which are your earliest warning of terlipressin- and albumin-associated pulmonary edema, and for focused cardiac views. But do not trust IVC collapsibility in tense ascites — ADQI/ICA 2024 warns POCUS is "prone to interobserver variability and challenging to use in patients with significant ascites," because the ascites mechanically alters IVC dynamics.
Support

Vasoactive agents

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose (HRS context)AccessWhen to pick
TerlipressinSelective V₁ₐ agonist; prodrug of lysine-vasopressin. Minimal V₂ activity, so less free-water retention than vasopressin0.85 mg IV q6h × 3 days → day 4: continue if creatinine fell ≥30%, escalate to 1.7 mg q6h if <30%, stop if at/above baseline. Max 1.7 mg q6h; max 14 daysPeripheral or central; bolus over 2 minFirst-line. The only FDA-approved drug for this indication
Norepinephrineα₁ ≫ β₁0.5 mg/h → +0.5 mg/h q4h → max 3 mg/h (≈8.3 → 50 mcg/min). Target MAP rise ≥10 mmHg or urine output >200 mL/4 hCentral line; ICU/step-downWhen terlipressin is unavailable or contraindicated — and first-line if there is concurrent septic shock, where one agent covers both problems
VasopressinV₁ₐ + V₂Typically 0.03 units/min fixed, added to norepinephrineCentral lineAdjunct in ACLF with septic shock as a norepinephrine-sparing agent. Not a substitute for terlipressin in HRS — it is not the studied agent, and V₂ activity worsens free-water retention and hyponatremia
Epinephrineα₁, β₁, β₂Titrated for refractory shockCentral lineRescue in refractory shock. Not an HRS therapy — β₂ vasodilation and lactate generation are unhelpful here
MidodrinePeripheral α₁ agonist (oral prodrug → desglymidodrine)7.5 mg PO TID → 12.5 mg PO TID (up to 15 mg TID); target MAP rise ≥15 mmHgOralWard-level third-line with octreotide; also used to wean off IV pressors and as an outpatient bridge
OctreotideSomatostatin analogue — inhibits splanchnic vasodilators (glucagon, VIP)100 → 200 mcg SC TID, or 50 mcg/h IVSC or IVAdjunct to midodrine only; essentially no independent efficacy
Albumin 25%Oncotic plus non-oncotic: binds NO, endotoxin, bilirubin, bile acids, reactive oxygen species1 g/kg day 1, then 20–40 g/day (AASLD text says 40–50 g/day)IVMandatory companion to every vasoconstrictor. Hold for volume overload
Sequencing logic. Terlipressin first if available and not contraindicated → norepinephrine if terlipressin is unavailable, contraindicated (hypoxia, ACLF-3, active ischemia) or if the patient is in concurrent septic shock → midodrine + octreotide only if neither is possible. All three are aiming at the same arrow in the cascade: re-narrow the splanchnic bed. They differ in potency and in what monitoring they demand, not in intent.
Renal

Renal replacement therapy

🩺

When, which modality, and — most importantly — why

AASLD 2021, verbatim: "The optimal timing for initiation of RRT has not been studied in patients with cirrhosis. Initiation of RRT should be made on clinical grounds, including worsening kidney function, electrolyte disturbances such as severe acidosis, hyponatremia or hyperkalemia not improving with medical management, diuretic intolerance, or increasing volume overload. Continuous RRT is the modality preferred to intermittent dialysis in patients who are hemodynamically unstable."

IndicationThreshold
Refractory hyperkalemiaK >6.5 mEq/L, or any potassium with ECG changes, not correcting medically
Severe metabolic acidosisArterial pH <7.2
Volume overloadRefractory to — or precluding — medical management. Especially the terlipressin patient who cannot safely receive albumin
Uremic complicationsPericarditis, bleeding, encephalopathy not attributable to HE
Severe refractory hyponatremiaIncluding periprocedural management around hypertonic saline before transplant

CRRT vs intermittent hemodialysis

  • CRRT for the hemodynamically unstable — an explicit AASLD statement. Gentler solute and volume removal preserves MAP on vasopressors.
  • CRRT also when cerebral edema is a concern — in HE grade 3–4 and ACLF, the rapid osmolar shifts of intermittent dialysis can precipitate or worsen cerebral edema. Slow continuous clearance avoids that physiology.
  • IHD is reasonable for the hemodynamically stable, non-encephalopathic patient and for those transitioning out of the unit.
Citrate anticoagulation in liver failure — the "citrate lock." Regional citrate anticoagulation is the default CRRT anticoagulant because of its low bleeding risk, but citrate is cleared by the hepatic Krebs cycle, which is impaired here, so it accumulates. Monitor the total-calcium to ionized-calcium ratio: a ratio ≥2.5 defines citrate accumulation. A rising ratio plus worsening metabolic acidosis plus an escalating systemic calcium requirement is citrate lock. Honest evidence: citrate anticoagulation remains feasible in severe liver dysfunction with protocolized monitoring — it is not absolutely contraindicated — but the ratio must be followed, and heparin-free or systemic-heparin CRRT is the fallback.
Do not start RRT on a creatinine number. STARRT-AKI (N=2,927) found 90-day mortality of 43.9% with accelerated vs 43.7% with standard initiation — no benefit — and among 90-day survivors, continued RRT dependence was higher in the accelerated arm (10.4% vs 6.0%). AKIKI reached the same conclusion. Start RRT for a complication, and toward a destination.
RRT in HRS is a bridge to transplant. AASLD: "Mortality rates are extremely high in patients not listed for LT who receive RRT, whether the AKI was due to HRS or ATN," and "Initiation of RRT in patients who are not candidates for LT must be made with a clear endpoint in mind." A limited trial may be reasonable in selected non-candidates depending on the reversibility of their other organ failures. But if you cannot state the endpoint out loud, RRT converts a dying patient into a dying patient on a machine. Say so, kindly, and early.
Airway

Respiratory support & ventilation

🌬️

When to intubate and initial settings

Intubate for: HE grade 3–4 (airway protection — grade 3 is somnolent but rousable with incomprehensible speech, grade 4 is coma; these patients aspirate) · terlipressin-associated respiratory failure, the boxed-warning event, whose median onset in CONFIRM was 4.5 days (IQR 2–7) · massive variceal bleeding before endoscopy · refractory hypoxemia with PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤200.

Mode
