The plateau-pressure trap in cirrhosis. Tense ascites and hepatic hydrothorax reduce chest-wall compliance, so a high plateau pressure may reflect the abdomen rather than the lung. Do not reflexively drop the tidal volume below the protective range to chase a plateau number — transpulmonary pressure is what injures lung. Consider large-volume paracentesis to improve respiratory mechanics in the ventilated patient with tense ascites (with albumin 6–8 g per liter removed when taking >5 L).
If you intubate a terlipressin patient for hypoxemia, terlipressin is now contraindicated. Hypoxia and worsening respiratory symptoms are label contraindications. Stop it and switch to norepinephrine — do not continue it through the intubation.

Avoid benzodiazepines where possible: they worsen encephalopathy and are unpredictably cleared. Propofol is generally preferred; dexmedetomidine is an option but hypotension limits it in the vasoplegic cirrhotic.

Rescue

Advanced & definitive therapy

⚙️

TIPS, albumin dialysis, and transplant

TIPS

AASLD 2021, verbatim: "TIPS is not recommended in patients with AKI-HRS because of insufficient information." The physiologic rationale is sound — TIPS decompresses the portal hypertension driving the whole cascade — but the HRS-AKI-specific evidence is small and uncontrolled. Two cautions are specific to this population: these patients frequently have cirrhotic cardiomyopathy (TIPS acutely increases preload and can precipitate decompensated heart failure) and ACLF. The EASL 2025 TIPS guideline states there is insufficient evidence to define an absolute creatinine, CKD stage, or RRT status that contraindicates TIPS, and recommends adjunct risk prediction instead (Freiburg index of post-TIPS survival, MELD 3.0).

Widely quoted numeric TIPS cutoffs — "bilirubin >5 mg/dL," "MELD >18" — are practice conventions, not guideline-endorsed absolute thresholds; EASL 2025 explicitly declines to set them. Do not quote them as fact. Liver-HERO (TIPS vs terlipressin + albumin in HRS-AKI, primary endpoint 12-month transplant-free survival) is the RCT designed to settle this; results were not published as of this build.

MARS / Prometheus — albumin dialysis

State it plainly: extracorporeal liver support does not improve survival.

  • RELIEF (N=189 ACLF, MARS vs standard medical therapy, up to ten 6–8 h sessions): a beneficial effect on survival could not be demonstrated. Acceptable safety, a real dialysis effect, and a non-significant improvement in severe HE.
  • HELIOS (N=145 ACLF, Prometheus fractionated plasma separation and adsorption vs standard therapy, 8–11 sessions over 3 weeks): no survival benefit at day 28 or 90.

Albumin dialysis is a device with a measurable physiologic effect and no proven survival benefit. It is not standard care for HRS-AKI — reserve it for research protocols or highly selected bridge-to-transplant cases at experienced centers.

Liver transplantation — the only definitive cure

AASLD: "Restoring liver function by LT is the ultimate therapy for HRS-AKI," and the guidance statement: "All patients with cirrhosis and AKI should be considered for urgent LT evaluation given the high short-term mortality even in responders to vasoconstrictors." Recovery of kidney function after transplant is not guaranteed — pre-existing CKD, diabetes, unrecognized intrinsic renal disease, intraoperative events and calcineurin-inhibitor nephrotoxicity all work against it.

Simultaneous liver–kidney (SLK) eligibility — OPTN/UNOS policy, effective 2017
Chronic kidney disease: eGFR ≤60 mL/min for >90 consecutive days, plus a subsequent eGFR ≤30 mL/min or dialysis at/after kidney waitlist registration
Sustained AKI: dialysis, or eGFR/CrCl ≤25 mL/min, for at least 6 consecutive weeks, documented at least every 7 days
Metabolic disease: hyperoxaluria, atypical HUS from factor H or factor I mutations, familial non-neuropathic systemic amyloidosis, methylmalonic aciduria
The "safety net": a patient who received a liver alone and is registered on the kidney waitlist between 60 and 365 days after transplant with eGFR/CrCl ≤20 mL/min or on chronic dialysis receives increased priority for a deceased-donor kidney

The safety net exists precisely so teams are not pressured to over-list for SLK: transplant the liver alone, give the kidney 2–12 months to recover, and retain prioritized access to a kidney if it does not.

The MELD paradox — discuss with transplant before you call pharmacy. AASLD: "Successful treatment of their AKI leads to a reduction in MELD score because of improvement in creatinine values, which disadvantages the patient, whereas the decrease in MELD may not translate to a meaningful gain in survival." Treating HRS successfully can move a listed patient down the waiting list without improving their true survival. Some countries address this by maintaining the pretreatment MELD or awarding exception points. In the US, this is a conversation to have with the transplant team before starting terlipressin in a listed patient.
What this actually looks like in the US. The HRS-HARMONY consortium (16 US academic centers, N=243, post-approval real-world practice) reported creatinine 2.79 mg/dL and MELD 31 at terlipressin initiation, overall response 55.1%, HRS reversal 30.9%, 90-day mortality 40.5%, and liver transplant by 90 days in 28.4%. Notably 49% met "extended criteria" — that is, were treated outside strict label or trial criteria, most commonly ACLF grade 3 (45%) — and adverse events including respiratory failure were more common when terlipressin was used outside label guidance. Nearly half of US use is off-label, and that is exactly where the harm concentrates.
Fluoroscopy during TIPS creation. TIPS is the one therapy that attacks the upstream step — portal pressure itself — rather than compensating downstream. It is established for refractory ascites and variceal bleeding, but not recommended once HRS-AKI has developed.
Samir, CC BY 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons, Fluoroscopic image of TIPS in progress.jpg
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when ALL of the following hold:

DomainCriterion
HemodynamicsOff vasopressors ≥12–24 h with MAP ≥65 mmHg, or on a ward-permissible regimen (peripheral terlipressin; midodrine/octreotide)
RespiratoryExtubated ≥24 h, SpO₂ ≥92% on ≤4 L nasal cannula, no rising oxygen requirement
NeurologicHE grade ≤2, airway protected, following commands
RenalCreatinine stable or improving × 48 h; if on RRT, converted to intermittent hemodialysis on a fixed schedule
MetabolicK <5.5 mEq/L, arterial pH ≥7.30, no large ongoing electrolyte swings
HematologicNo active bleeding; hemoglobin stable × 24 h
InfectiousSource controlled, on a defined antibiotic course, afebrile and off vasopressors
Not yet if…
  • Still on terlipressin with any downtrending SpO₂, new dyspnea, or a new infiltrate — this is the boxed-warning window (days 2–7). Keep them monitored.
  • Norepinephrine at any dose — at most institutions this is not a ward drug; step-down at best, and only under an explicit protocol.
  • HE grade 3–4, or fluctuating mental status without a secured airway.
  • CRRT running, or hemodynamic instability on intermittent hemodialysis.
  • ACLF grade 3 with ongoing organ-failure progression — 28-day mortality 76.7%.
  • Any ischemic complication on a vasoconstrictor (digital, mesenteric, cardiac) that has not fully resolved.
  • Awaiting an imminent transplant offer where rapid deterioration would change candidacy.
  • Goals of care not yet established in a non-transplant candidate with no response at day 4. That conversation belongs before the transfer, not after.
Shared

Clinical pearls

💡

The things that change what you do

1 · Creatinine lies in cirrhosis, and it lies in the direction that hurts you. Reduced hepatic creatine synthesis, sarcopenia, an expanded volume of distribution, and bilirubin interference with Jaffe assays all push it down. By the time creatinine is clearly abnormal, GFR has already collapsed — and terlipressin response falls from 49.2% at baseline creatinine <3 mg/dL to 9.1% at ≥5 mg/dL. The lag costs you the drug.

2 · Treat early — the 48-hour rule is a guideline, not a physical law. AASLD requires no response after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal plus albumin, but also says AKI "should be treated as soon as possible." The 2024 ADQI/ICA consensus formally recommends against requiring the 48-hour albumin trial for diagnosis. The eTerli RCT (N=70) started terlipressin at 12 h versus 48 h in ACLF with stage II/III AKI: day-7 full response 68.6% vs 31.4%, 28-day mortality 40% vs 65.7%.

3 · FENa is useless here, and most of these patients are on diuretics anyway. FENa and FEUrea could not differentiate prerenal AKI from HRS-AKI (AUC <70%), and ADQI/ICA 2024 notes FENa <1% is common in cirrhosis even without AKI. A high FENa (>2%) is informative — it argues for ATN. A low one tells you almost nothing. Note that AASLD's criteria pointedly use proteinuria, hematuria and ultrasound instead.

4 · Look at the urine sediment yourself. It is free, immediate, and the highest-yield discriminator you have. Muddy-brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cell casts mean ATN. Green-brown bile-stained casts mean bile cast nephropathy — found in 44.8% of post-mortem renal biopsies in HRS-related AKI and 74.4% in ACLF. Neither responds to terlipressin.

5 · Above a creatinine of 5 mg/dL, terlipressin is not just futile — it is harmful. The label states patients above 5 mg/dL "are unlikely to experience benefit" (reversal 9.1%), and a practical review reports fatal adverse events of 66% with terlipressin vs 39% with placebo in that group. You would be exposing a patient to boxed-warning toxicity for a 1-in-11 chance of benefit.

6 · The ACLF-3 harm signal is real and it is in the boxed warning. ACLF grade 3 means ≥3 organ failures and a 28-day mortality of 76.7%. Use norepinephrine instead. The tension with Arora 2020 — which found terlipressin superior to norepinephrine in ACLF — resolves on grade: the harm sits at grade 3, not across all ACLF.

7 · Albumin is not just an oncotic agent, and it is not free. It binds endotoxin, bilirubin, nitric oxide and reactive oxygen species, which is the mechanistic argument for ANSWER's 18-month survival benefit (77% vs 66%, HR 0.62) in outpatient ascites. But ATTIRE pushed albumin to a target in hospitalized decompensated cirrhotics and found no benefit and more severe or life-threatening adverse events from pulmonary edema and fluid overload. Over-albuminizing today also makes the patient ineligible for terlipressin tomorrow.

8 · The beta-blocker window — the common error is never restarting it. Hold for SBP <90, Na <130, creatinine >1.5, or MAP <65 with SBP. But AASLD is explicit that NSBBs "might be reintroduced if circulatory dysfunction improves." A patient discharged permanently off a beta-blocker is a patient unprotected from variceal bleeding.

9 · SBP prophylaxis prevents HRS better than any drug treats it. Fernández 2007: norfloxacin in high-risk cirrhotics cut 1-year SBP from 61% to 7%, 1-year HRS from 41% to 28%, and raised 3-month survival from 62% to 94%. Note that norfloxacin was withdrawn from the US market in 2014 — in US practice this means ciprofloxacin or TMP-SMX.

10 · Tap every cirrhotic with ascites who is admitted, within 12 hours, for any reason. Early diagnostic paracentesis is associated with lower in-hospital mortality (OR 0.51 within 12 h; OR 0.67 within 24 h), and performing one at all carried an adjusted OR 0.55. Coagulopathy is not a contraindication and clotting factors should not be transfused to cover it — cirrhosis is a rebalanced hemostatic state, not a hypocoagulable one.

11 · Do not transfuse above a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL. Villanueva 2013 (N=921): restrictive versus liberal transfusion in severe upper GI bleeding gave 6-week survival 95% vs 91% (HR for death 0.55) with less rebleeding (10% vs 16%). Over-transfusion raises portal pressure and precipitates rebleeding.

12 · Response is not cure — transplant is. CONFIRM showed no mortality benefit (90-day mortality 51% vs 45%) despite improving renal outcomes; REVERSE missed its primary endpoint entirely. Reversal behaves more like a prognostic marker than a cure. AASLD: all patients with cirrhosis and AKI should get an urgent transplant evaluation, even the responders.

13 · Watch out for the MELD paradox. Successfully treating HRS lowers the creatinine, lowers the MELD, and can push a listed patient down the waiting list without a matching survival gain. Talk to the transplant team before starting terlipressin in a listed patient.

14 · Do not put in a Foley just to measure urine output. AASLD, verbatim: "Indwelling bladder catheterization should be avoided." Catheter-associated infection is a direct HRS precipitant in a patient whose entire prognosis turns on avoiding infection. Urine volume genuinely matters — solve it with a condom catheter, weighed pads, or scheduled straight catheterization.

15 · Do not use terlipressin as a diagnostic test. The AGA 2024 update advises explicitly against giving it to "see whether the creatinine moves." That exposes a patient who may have ATN or bile cast nephropathy to respiratory failure and ischemia for no possible benefit.

16 · Never titrate lactulose to an ammonia level. AASLD's HE guidance: "high blood-ammonia levels alone do not add any diagnostic, staging, or prognostic value." Titrate to 2–3 soft stools per day and mental status. Over-titration causes hypovolemic, hypernatremic losses that both cause and mimic HRS.

17 · Correct hyponatremia slowly — cirrhosis is a maximal-risk state for osmotic demyelination. Malnutrition, alcohol use, hypokalemia and chronicity all stack. Fluid restriction to 1,000 mL/day for moderate hyponatremia; note AASLD's realism that a meaningful rise generally requires intake <750 mL/day, which is "very poorly tolerated." Correct hypokalemia too — potassium counts toward your correction rate. Vaptans are not standard care: the FDA limits tolvaptan to 30 days with a boxed warning for hepatocellular injury, and the sodium effect does not persist.

18 · RRT without a destination is not a treatment. Start it for a complication (K >6.5, pH <7.2, refractory volume overload, uremia) and toward a destination (transplant, or a time-limited trial with an agreed stopping point). AASLD notes mortality is "extremely high in patients not listed for LT who receive RRT."

Guidelines & consensus documents

  • AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance — the primary source for this guide. Biggins SW, Angeli P, Garcia-Tsao G, Ginès P, Ling SC, Nadim MK, Wong F, Kim WR. "Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Management of Ascites, Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis and Hepatorenal Syndrome." Hepatology 2021;74(2):1014–1048. doi:10.1002/hep.31884 · PubMed. Note: this document predates the September 2022 FDA approval of terlipressin and states the drug "is not yet approved in United States" — dose from the label, not from here.
  • ADQI / ICA joint consensus 2024 — the newest criteria. Nadim MK, Kellum JA, Forni L, Francoz C, et al. "Acute kidney injury in patients with cirrhosis: Acute Disease Quality Initiative (ADQI) and International Club of Ascites (ICA) joint multidisciplinary consensus meeting." J Hepatol 2024. Full text (PMC) · PubMed. Source of the urine-output criterion and of the recommendation against a mandatory 48-hour albumin trial.
  • FDA TERLIVAZ (terlipressin) prescribing information, NDA 022231, approved 14 September 2022. DailyMed label. The legally binding US dosing document — source of every terlipressin dose, the boxed warning and the contraindications on this page.
  • ICA 2015 revised consensus. Angeli P, et al. "Diagnosis and management of acute kidney injury in patients with cirrhosis: revised consensus recommendations of the International Club of Ascites." J Hepatol 2015;62(4):968–974. Full text
  • EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines for the management of patients with decompensated cirrhosis. J Hepatol 2018;69(2):406–460. PDF · PubMed
  • AASLD 2024 Practice Guidance on portal hypertension and varices — source of the carvedilol/propranolol/nadolol dose ladders. Kaplan DE, Bosch J, Ripoll C, Thiele M, Fortune BE, Simonetto DA, Garcia-Tsao G. Hepatology 2024;79(5):1180–1211.
  • AASLD 2024 Practice Guidance on Acute-on-Chronic Liver Failure and the Management of Critically Ill Patients with Cirrhosis. Karvellas CJ, Bajaj JS, Kamath PS, Napolitano L, O'Leary JG, Solà E, et al. Hepatology 2024;79(6):1463–1502. The current document for the ICU half of cirrhosis care.
  • Baveno VII consensus. de Franchis R, Bosch J, Garcia-Tsao G, Reiberger T, Ripoll C. J Hepatol 2022;76(4):959–974. Established carvedilol as the preferred NSBB.
  • AGA Clinical Practice Update — Vasoactive Drugs and IV Albumin in Cirrhosis, Gastroenterology, January 2024. Source of the recommendation against using terlipressin as a diagnostic test, and of the statement that continuous infusion is not an approved US route.
  • AGA Clinical Practice Update — Ascites, Volume Overload and Hyponatremia in Cirrhosis, Gastroenterology, October 2025.
  • EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on TIPS, J Hepatol 2025 — declines to set absolute renal contraindications to TIPS.
  • USPSTF: Hepatitis C screening, Grade B, 2020 · Hepatitis B screening in at-risk adults, Grade B, 2020 · Unhealthy alcohol use screening, Grade B, 2018
  • Child-Turcotte-Pugh score — point values as used in the calculator: StatPearls, "Use of the Child Pugh Score in Liver Disease". (Note: the albumin thresholds are in g/dL — some secondary sources misprint the unit.)
  • MDCalc — scores deliberately not reimplemented here: MELD 3.0 · MELD-Na · Child-Pugh

Deliberate omissions — stated so you can trust the rest

  • MELD 3.0 / MELD-Na are linked out, not reimplemented — continuous logarithmic formulas with sex and interaction terms, where a silent transcription error would be dangerous.
  • No numeric TIPS contraindication cutoffs are given. EASL 2025 explicitly declines to set absolute renal thresholds; the widely quoted "bilirubin >5" and "MELD >18" figures are practice conventions, not guideline statements.
  • No numeric mEq/L per 24 h sodium-correction ceiling is attributed to AASLD. AASLD 2021 describes rapid versus gradual correction qualitatively but publishes no numeric ceiling; the familiar ≤8 and ≤10–12 mEq/24 h limits come from the general hyponatremia literature.
  • The "albumin maximum 100 g/day" cap is labeled as practice convention — the 1 g/kg/day dose is verbatim AASLD, but the 100 g ceiling is not stated in that document.
  • Symptom frequencies marked "~" or "common" are typical-range estimates, not cohort-derived, and are labeled as such in the presentation table.
